report.source_text: The blood test revealed a white cell count of 3100/μL (normal range 4000–9000/μL). Her haemoglobin was 6.9 g/dL (normal range 13.5–17.6 g/dL). Her mean corpuscular volume (MCV) could not be measured because of significant haemolysis; however, there was no erythrocyte fragmentation in her peripheral blood smear. The platelet count was 16×109/L (normal range 150×109–400×109/L). Aspartate aminotransferase was 1905 IU/L (normal range 7–97 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase was 690 IU/L (normal range 6–43 IU/L), total bilirubin was 8.1 mg/dL (normal range 0.3–1.2 mg/dL), blood urea nitrogen was 27.0 mg/dL (normal range 10–20 mg/dL) and creatinine was 2.0 mg/dL (normal range 0.6–1.0 mg/dL); that is, liver and kidney dysfunctions were also observed. The blood glucose level was 278 mg/dL. The prothrombin time–international normalised ratio was 2.82 (normal range 0.85–1.15), activated partial thromboplastin time was 54.6 s (normal range 24.3–36.0 s), fibrinogen was 130.1 mg/dL (normal range 150–400 mg/dL) and D-dimer was 195.4 µg/mL (normal range <1.0 µg/mL). In a urine test, her urine had macroscopic haematuria. These data and a bleeding tendency showed disseminated intravascular coagulation.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%) presented with a 3-day history of fever followed by altered consciousness 1 day prior to admission. On presentation, she was febrile (40.5°C), tachycardic (HR 120), tachypneic (RR 50), and jaundiced with hemoptysis and pan-inspiratory crackles. Laboratory studies revealed severe intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL with inability to measure MCV due to hemolysis and absence of schistocytes on blood smear), thrombocytopenia (16×10⁹/L), markedly elevated transaminases (AST 1905, ALT 690), hyperbilirubinemia (8.1 mg/dL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.0, BUN 27), and disseminated intravascular coagulation (PT-INR 2.82, aPTT 54.6, fibrinogen 130.1, D-dimer 195.4). Macroscopic hematuria was present. Giemsa staining of blood smear showed Bacillus phagocytosed by leucocytes, consistent with bacteremia. Postmortem CT imaging revealed a gas-forming liver abscess as the source of infection. The patient rapidly deteriorated and suffered cardiac arrest 1 hour after hospital presentation, despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
